Styles / 06 / Pilot

Neo-brutalism

A web and interface style of the 2020s: flat bright fills, thick black outlines, hard offset shadows with no blur, large bold type, and components that look like physical blocks.

Direct / Loud / Playful / Raw

Visual grammar

  • Thick outlines. Every card, button, and input has a 2 to 4 px black border.
  • Hard shadows. Solid black shadows offset down and right, with no blur. Pressed buttons move into their shadow.
  • Flat brights. Yellow, pink, mint, lilac, and orange fills on off-white or white.
  • Heavy display type. Large, bold grotesque or geometric sans-serif headings. Sometimes monospaced labels.
  • Blocky layout. Components stack as distinct blocks with visible edges. Little overlap, little transparency.

What connects the references

Two articles define the style: Malewicz (2022) and NN/g (2025). Both name Gumroad’s 2021 redesign as a key example.

Open-source component libraries turn the style into reusable parts: neobrutalism components for React, a SwiftUI package, a Flutter package, RetroUI, and Snowball’s Fractal design system.

Captures of real sites calibrated the fingerprint. The component-library sites pass it: neobrutalism.dev, neobrutalism.com, BoldKit, and the Neubrutalism guide. Brand sites apply the style more loosely. The archived Gumroad home page has outlines and flat brights but no shadows at rest, Figma 2022 shows neither outlines nor hard shadows, and Snowball uses 1 px outlines. Hard shadows are most consistent in component libraries.

The live Gumroad, Zama, and cc creative sites, which earlier lists cited as examples, no longer use the style on 25 September 2026. Web references date quickly, so cite archived copies with a date.

Identity

Name
Name used by designers and vendors
Also called
Neubrutalism, Neo brutalism
Era
2021–present. Gumroad announced its redesign on 26 November 2021. Malewicz described the trend in March 2022.
Regions
International
Name used by
Michał Malewicz, “Neubrutalism is taking over the web” (2022), Nielsen Norman Group, “Neobrutalism: Definition and Best Practices” (2025), Envato, “Trend Deep Dive: Neo-brutalism” (2023)

Lineage

  • Descends from Brutalist web design. Earlier deliberately raw websites, which used default HTML, visible structure, and no polish.
  • Related to Brutalist architecture. The connection is by name and attitude: exposed structure and raw material. It is not a visual descent.
  • Reaction against Flat design. A common reading: it keeps flat color but brings back strong edges and depth through hard shadows.
  • Related to Memphis. Shares bright, playful color. Memphis relies on pattern, neo-brutalism on outlines and shadows.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • Most components have thick black outlines.
  • Shadows are solid and offset with no blur.
  • Fills are flat, bright colors.
  • Headings are large and heavy.

Rules it out

  • Soft, blurred shadows or glass effects.
  • Thin hairline borders or no borders.
  • Muted or monochrome palettes with gradients.

Often confused with

Brutalist web design
Brutalist web design is raw and often default-styled. Neo-brutalism is a polished, colorful system with outlines and hard shadows.
Memphis
Memphis uses patterns and irregular shapes. Neo-brutalism uses outlined rectangles and hard shadows.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Give every interactive element a 2 to 3 px solid black border.
  • Use a hard shadow such as 4px 4px 0 black. On press, move the element 4 px down and right and remove the shadow.
  • Fill cards and buttons with flat bright colors. Keep text black for contrast.
  • Use a heavy sans-serif for headings at large sizes.
  • Keep corners square or slightly rounded, up to 8 px.

Keep the function

  • Do not blur shadows or use gradients.
  • Do not use thin gray borders. The outline must read as a strong black line.
  • Do not use more than one pastel as a large background.

Useful directions: creator tools, startups, portfolios, developer products.
